title: Treatment of infantile hemangioma
what: A hemangioma is a harmless blood vessel mark in babies. It usually grows in the first months and then slowly shrinks on its own. Sometimes it is treated.
why: When a hemangioma grows quickly, is near the eye, lips or nose, is in a place that rubs, or breaks open.
duration: the visit usually takes 20 to 30 minutes; treatment usually takes months
tell_doctor: When it appeared and how fast it is growing
Whether there have been sores or bleeding on the mark
Whether your baby has heart or breathing problems or low blood sugar
All of your baby's medicines and supplements

prepare.title: Photos
prepare.text: Take a photo of the mark from the side with a ruler next to it - this shows whether it is growing.

prepare.title: Decision
prepare.text: Whether to wait or treat is up to the doctor. Sometimes it is treated with pills, sometimes with a laser.

prepare.title: Pills
prepare.text: If pills are prescribed, the first dose is often given under the doctor's watch.

bring: Photos of the mark from the last few weeks
A list of questions for the doctor
A bottle, or the breast - to calm your baby
steps: The doctor examines the mark and measures it
If needed, prescribes pills or a laser
Laser: your baby's eyes are protected and the mark is treated with short flashes
feel: Laser feels like a rubber band snap, and the skin is cooled; your baby may cry
after: If pills are prescribed, give them with food and at the same time every day
Do not stop the pills on your own
Photograph the mark once a week or every two weeks
red_flags: The mark bleeds or a sore appears - see a doctor
The mark makes it hard to open the eye or to breathe - see a doctor urgently
On pills: your baby is limp, pale, sweaty or feeding poorly - call your local emergency number

faq.q: Will a hemangioma go away by itself?
faq.a: Often it shrinks on its own over a few years. The doctor decides if treatment is needed.
Usually not. It is a concern if it affects the eye or breathing, or bleeds.

reminders.text: Hemangioma visit tomorrow. Take photos of the mark and your baby's medical record.
